The post Review: 2025 Harken Chardonnay California appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The ABC (Anything but Chardonnay) movement didn’t really take hold the way some people would have hoped. All of its most boisterous vocal proponents either set off to the great big vineyard in the sky or moved on to putting Merlot or Rosé on blast. But certain Chardonnays are serving as proof of victory, and Harken’s Chardonnay is one of them. Like most eccentric Californians, they are fully committed to the bit of doing one thing well and are wholly unbothered by media trends. Harken simply does Chardonnay and that’s that.

The nose opens with an expected roll call of citrus: orange, lemon, and pear, eventually followed by vanilla from oak aging arriving just a few beats behind. On the palate, pear carries through, joined by roasted nuts and a rich, custardy quality reminiscent of crème brulèe. This isn’t a lean, mineral-driven Chardonnay by any stretch, and it leans fully into a rich sweetness. The finish is long and citrus-forward, with a thin thread of minerality appearing late that provides balance and contrast against the buttery, oak-driven weight of everything that came before.

This is a classic old-school California Chardonnay. The kind people either adore or pretend to have grown out of during social gatherings. It’s also an unquestionably genuine bargain, making it feel less of a guilty pleasure and more like a good call for the bank balance. Crack it open in late October or early November, paired with roasted root vegetables, and let it do what it’s been aiming to do: strut its stuff with pride.

B+ / $16

title: Review: Redwood Empire The Hyperion
summary:

The post Review: Redwood Empire The Hyperion appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Bay Area, California-based Redwood Empire recently dropped a new limited edition offering dubbed “The Hyperion,” named after the world’s tallest living tree in California’s Redwood National Park, which it calls its most ambitious project yet. What’s in the bottle? A little bit of everything.

Creating “The Hyperion” Batch 001 began, intentionally, without an established path. Redwood Empire’s Master Distiller-Master Blender duo explored a broad terrain of mature barrels, crossing the traditional boundaries separating bourbon, rye, wheat whiskey, and single malt whiskey. The resulting 110-proof expression brings together four distinct whiskey categories, more than 10 mashbills, and stocks aged from 7 to 14 years, arriving at a destination no single whiskey could reach on its own.

“The Hyperion is an exercise in artistry. Regal, refined, bold. A collaboration of spirit types that fully brings to light the depth and diversity of our barrel inventory,” said Lauren Patz, Master Blender at Redwood Empire Whiskey. “Wheat Whiskey, Bourbon, Rye, and American Single Malt find both balance and transformation and demonstrate what can emerge when curiosity is matched with patience and purpose.”

In lieu of a traditional mash bill, the inaugural label instead boasts a blend bill—a collection of whiskey blends, rather than simply mashes—of 32% bourbon whiskey, 30% rye whiskey, 25% wheat whiskey, and 13% single malt whiskey. The final blend of approximately 79 barrels combines multiple mash bills from curated whiskey stocks from Redwood Empire and other distillers in Indiana, Kentucky, and Tennessee. Each category combines multiple mash bills from a total of 50-100 barrels of curated whiskey stocks from Redwood Empire and others distilled in Indiana, Kentucky, and Tennessee. The single malt component is entirely grain-to-glass whiskey distilled by Redwood Empire. The blended whiskey entered the barrel between 110 and 120 proof and matured in toasted, Char No. 3 barrels. Maturation takes place in Northern California, where warm days give way to fog-laced cool winds off the Pacific at night.

Whoa.

Also dig the wooden bottle stopper, another unique and very cool touch to cap off an interesting spirit.

Redwood Empire The Hyperion Review

The whiskey noses with the expected complexity, but sweetness dominates. Vanilla syrup, short of cake frosting but getting there, meanders toward chocolate syrup, raspberry glaze, and a stone fruit compote. Increasingly spicy and nutty as it gets a bit of air, the whiskey’s buttery core never loses any steam at all.

The palate finds many of the same elements but ups the ante further. Sweet and buttery, it drinks like well-slathered cinnamon toast, almost syrupy in texture at times. Coconut is dominant on the midpalate, again creamy to the point where it feels like it could fit in in a pina colada. This lingers for ages before segueing toward milk chocolate, caramel, and toffee notes, with touches of brown banana creating something of a banana split character. Dollops of whipped cream top things off.

All told, this is a far sunnier and sweeter whiskey than I was expecting, perhaps unexpectedly driven by the wheat whiskey in the blend. I’m not mad at it.

Reviewed: Batch 1. 110 proof.

A- / $99

title: Tasting Report: Malbecs for Fall 2026
summary:
Every declining empire eventually presents the same magic trick: debase the currency while publicly insisting it has never held higher value and reverence. American wine pricing has absorbed the lesson well. Malbec, a grape spending most of its history as a humble tenant in the cellars of the working class, continues to experience inflation normally…

The post Tasting Report: Malbecs for Fall 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Every declining empire eventually presents the same magic trick: debase the currency while publicly insisting it has never held higher value and reverence. American wine pricing has absorbed the lesson well. Malbec, a grape spending most of its history as a humble tenant in the cellars of the working class, continues to experience inflation normally reserved for the 100-point Parkeratti of Wine. Bottles once asking a reasonable price now demand tribute. Prestige labels, the aristocracy of any bull market, have taken to pricing themselves like sovereign debt.

Somehow, supply multiplies in obedience to demand, as it always does in the final stages of any speculative romance. What inflation has purchased, at least, are certain improvements. Ambitious producers are rewarded and quality continues to elevate. The conversation around Malbec is no longer the exclusive property of France and Argentina but can now also be claimed by domestic upstarts minting their own currency. Thankfully, good value can still be found by those willing to audit the books.

Now in its second year, we present an autumnal audit of recent Malbecs, from everyday considerations to the ostensibly cellar-worthy, in preparation for cold months and potentially even colder experiences with relatives during the holidays.

2025 Mendoza Vineyards Heroes Malbec Lujan de Cuyo – Created in tribute to the Argentina Men’s National Team for the 2026 World Cup. Unlike that team, this offering does not fall short of expectations: cherry, dark chocolate and coal running throughout, with herbs and a bit of soil eventually cutting through. Also unlike that team, this has a classy finish which lingers nicely and doesn’t attempt to start fights after the final whistle. One to pick up if you’re still in mourning, or cellar for the next four years. There’s always hope things will get better from here.  A- / $50

2021 Nico Malbec Gualtallary – Not to be confused with the Nico line produced by Luca (I know). Another year brings yet another expression to the expansive portfolio of Laura Catena and crew. Deep notes of raspberry and cherry run throughout, along with layers of blueberry, thyme, cassis and a touch of menthol. Nothing here really stands out and everyone plays together nicely. Traces of cedar plank also appear on the finish, allowing savory elements to amplify. It needs a bit of time and air, but once this finds its footing, it’s a wine that will endear itself to the most devoted Malbec mavens. Stacks up against its siblings commanding double the price, and one to open during a celebration in the cooler months. Quite lovely.  A / $120

2024 Zuccardi Concreto Malbec Valle du Uco – Without the reliance of oak barrel aging, this Zuccardi skips the dark fruit jam session and showcases herbaceous and mineral notes on the nose. The dark fruit eventually comes into focus on the palate, full of juicy plum and raspberry. However, that minerality returns in a big way on the finish. It’s a lively Malbec just slightly off the beaten path, and shows just how versatile and beautiful Malbec can be in the hands of a competence.  A- / $45

2020 Château de Mercuès Les Evêques Malbec Cahors – The brooding quality and boldness of this Vigouroux offering is usually reserved for the heaviest of Mendoza malbecs, and not something one would normally expect from the French. Blackberry, plum and Lapsang tea form a dense core that runs throughout, with a palate that recedes ever so slightly with an appearance of dark cherry on the palate and a finish providing a tinge of campfire smoke. Drink now if your curiosity gets the best of you, but allow for an adequate amount of time before serving. Otherwise, keep this around for 2028.  A- / $35

2022 Illaria Malbec Napa Valley – A Malbec-Cabernet Sauvignon blend of 84% and 16%, respectively. Initially dense with blackberry and blueberry, it eventually opens up with layers of dark chocolate, raspberry and rosemary. The oak pulls its weight on the finish, with touches of vanilla, graphite pencil and minerality lingering. This has aged 22 months in the barrel, and would likely do well with an equal measure of time in the cellar. B+ / $50

2023 Trivento Golden Reserve Malbec Lujan de Cuyo – There is a familiar and appealing medley immediately present that Malbec fans will appreciate: big notes of cherry and plum with cola, blackberry and chocolate all making appearances over time. Moderate acidity and tannins give this a good structure and make it a sensible weeknight pairing with a quick and easy meal off the grill to show off some of its charms. Still consistent and an excellent value purchase. For now. B+ / $20

2025 Domaine Bousquet Reserve Organic Malbec – Domaine Bousquet has made some branding changes over the years to their expansive lineup, so it may be hard to tell what is what without looking closely. However, this one stays the same and is all the better for it: dark fruit, baking spice and cedar work their way to a palate big on berries and earthy notes. The good acidity keeps matters from turning too beefy, and the floral lift keeps it easy drinking. A dependable release that hasn’t really increased in price over the years. Picking up one to age, one to have on hand to entertain uninvited house guests and one for now isn’t the worst idea.  B+ / $22

2024 Waterbrook Malbec Columbia Valley – Sometimes Malbec can show up being big, purple-faced and loud: the equivalent of a sweat-drenched guy who chicken-struts off the dance floor at a wedding to scream-explain cryptocurrency to everyone within earshot at the open bar. Westbrook doesn’t do this. It shows up lighter-bodied but still comes fully stocked with personality and restraint. Opening aromas of raspberry compote and blueberry threaten to make this a fruit bomb. But the threat is diffused on the palate, where darker tones of blackberry and black tea meld with violet and dark chocolate amidst good acidity and gentle tannins. A rare find of quality and affordability in a domestic market that leans overblown and inflated.  B+ / $20

2022 L’Atelier Crocus Malbec Cahors – A collaboration between Paul Hobbs and Gabriel Vigouroux. Intense blackcurrant supported by strawberry makes for a less-than-silent introduction, with notes of black pepper and plum as it winds its way to the finish, where a mild touch of chocolate settles things down nicely. Give this a year or so tucked away somewhere and the dividend will pay off.  B / $22

2023 OG de Négoce Lot 518 Napa Valley Malbec – I got this wrong. I was hoping that a year or so tucked away would yield improved results. It did not. This Napa Valley interpretation of a traditional Mendoza Malbec didn’t really move the needle in a positive direction, and it the dark fruit compote still dominates over all else. It’s a perfectly serviceable bottle, but it doesn’t really stand out in the crowd the way something from Napa ought to.  B / $22

2023 Trivento White Malbec Mendoza – Affordable and slightly unassuming, notes of white flower and herbs are evident at the start. However, with a bit of time, the wine develops more dimension to reveal a citrus edge of guava and hints of mango. It’s approachable and quite youthful, and one to have around that is more of a curiosity than a go-to.  B- / $13

2024 La Posta Pizzella Malbec Mendoza – A perennial everyday Malbec staple for years in our house, this year’s vintage failed to meet the standard. The hallmark raspberry and violet notes on the nose are still there, as is the plum, pepper and spice on the palate. But it never seems to really sort itself out and results in a jammy, overbearing affair. If possible, seek out older vintages.  C / $18

2025 Be Calm Malbec Argentina – All the usual suspects are present and accounted for: blackberry, plum, cinnamon, pepper and pencil shavings. However, it is so watered down that it becomes a laborious, sometimes painful, chore to even slow sip this. Best served in a chilled glass. Then, calmly, pour that glass straight down the drain immediately, muttering a silent apology to the drainage pipes.  D / $10

title: Review: Parker’s Heritage Collection Kentucky Straight Bourbon with Rye Backset 14 Years Old (2026)
summary:
The 20th edition of Heaven Hill Distillery’s Parker’s Heritage Collection Limited Edition bottling reads a bit strangely on paper, but I promise it’s easier than the convoluted name suggests. First, the broad technical details: Comprised of 100 barrels, the 20th Edition is made from Heaven Hill’s traditional Bourbon mashbill of 78% corn, 10% rye and…

The post Review: Parker’s Heritage Collection Kentucky Straight Bourbon with Rye Backset 14 Years Old (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The 20th edition of Heaven Hill Distillery’s Parker’s Heritage Collection Limited Edition bottling reads a bit strangely on paper, but I promise it’s easier than the convoluted name suggests.

First, the broad technical details:

Comprised of 100 barrels, the 20th Edition is made from Heaven Hill’s traditional Bourbon mashbill of 78% corn, 10% rye and 12% malted barley. Distilled between October 2011 and January 2012, the whiskey was aged for 14 years across four rickhouses and multiple floors: Rickhouse A on the second floor; Rickhouse KK on the first and second floors; and Rickhouses L and M on the third floor.

The twist comes with the bit about the “rye backset,” which refers to the portion of the liquid left after a distillation run that is traditionally reused in the next batch to improve consistency of flavor from batch to batch. Here, the backset used is rye whiskey, not bourbon, which was one of Parker Beam’s signature moves. It’s uncommon today, however, which makes this release particularly intriguing.

“Parker understood that the smallest details in the whiskey making process can have a meaningful impact on the final pour,” said Conor O’Driscoll, Heaven Hill Master Distiller. “This edition reflects that belief, using rye backset to create a 14-year-old Bourbon with remarkable depth, balance and spice. We’re proud to honor Parker’s enduring influence through a release that celebrates his steadfast belief in making the highest quality whiskey.”

As always, a portion of proceeds support the ALS Association, the disease with which Beam was diagnosed in 2010 and ultimately perished from.

I’m ready to tuck in to Parker’s Heritage XX. Here goes.

Parker’s Heritage Collection Kentucky Straight Bourbon with Rye Backset 14 Years Old (2026) Review

Let’s be frank: A rye backset means there’s more than a little rye in the finished product here, and it’s awfully hard to miss. Spice of both the baking and savory variety is heavy on the nose, though the aroma is also quite sweet, evoking elements of tangerine juice, fresh honey, and sweet tea. It’s a little tight at first blush (at 59% abv, that’s understandable), and a healthy splash of water helps decode the nose a bit more clearly, turning out more traditional notes of vanilla and milk chocolate.

The palate’s sweetness is immediate and, even given the foreshadowing of the nose, a little surprising. Golden syrup, touched with citrus, mixed florals, and vanilla custard are all dominant, with cinnamon-heavy spice building as the midpalate takes hold. This mixes with a latent barrel char quality that adds some back-of-palate grittiness to the experience, and while it isn’t overbearing, it does stick with you, coating the throat with a red pepper urgency.

Time in glass (and more water) help coax out more nuance. That black tea segues into green tea, with notes of tobacco becoming more forceful on the surprisingly pushy, lengthy finish.

I spent a long while noodling over this whiskey, which is entirely engaging and always enjoyable, but which felt like it might be struggling to tell its story with complete coherence. The punch of rye spice is more than evident, but there’s so much exuberant sweetness to balance it out that neither side of the equation ever completely takes over. Perhaps it was pulled a few years too early? That’s something I rarely say at the double-digit age level.

This is a whiskey that has been clinging to me for hours, long after I’ve washed my Glencairn. Part of me is still processing.

118 proof.

A- / $200

title: Review: Varvaglione 2023 Susumaniello Rosso Puglia and 2022 Papale Primitivo di Manduria DOP Linea Oro
summary:
A regional pride emerges in places the rest of the wine world spent a century overlooking on the way to somewhere more famous. Puglia (Apulia) is one of those areas. It stands as the bottom of Italy’s boot, doing the unglamorous work of growing things sun-baked and historically responsible for supplying the country’s bulk wine…

The post Review: Varvaglione 2023 Susumaniello Rosso Puglia and 2022 Papale Primitivo di Manduria DOP Linea Oro appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
A regional pride emerges in places the rest of the wine world spent a century overlooking on the way to somewhere more famous. Puglia (Apulia) is one of those areas. It stands as the bottom of Italy’s boot, doing the unglamorous work of growing things sun-baked and historically responsible for supplying the country’s bulk wine needs while Tuscany and Piedmont earned the magazine covers. Salento, the heel of that boot, is where the Varvaglione family set up shop in 1921. The founding myth here is modest: a guy named Cosimo, some vines outside Pulsano, and no particular ambition beyond keeping his own household in wine. Word got out, and it wasn’t long before sailors stationed at the nearby naval base were knocking on his door, which is its own kind of five-star review: nothing moves bottles quite like a fleet of bored, off-duty people in the military. One century and four generations later, the operation has grown considerably, but it hasn’t drifted. Today, we check in with two of their flagship offerings.

2023 Varvaglione Susumaniello Rosso Puglia – Quite dense and full-bodied, this wine heavily front-loads spice and balsamic and leans heavily into savory, earthy notes of mushroom and black pepper with time in the glass. Strawberry and black cherry come into focus on the palate as it develops, balancing the savory qualities that push so heavily up front. The finish is unwilling to go lightly, and revisits the balsamic thesis, accompanied by a coda of cocoa powder and black cherry. This is not a wine for idle company or light fare: it’s brooding and needs to be served with something substantial. B+ / $27

2022 Varvaglione Papale Primitivo di Manduria DOP Linea Oro – This 100% Primitivo di Manduria is an intense blend of rhubarb, cherry compote and tobacco leaf straight through, with orange zest and raspberry making intermittent appearances on the palate. The rhubarb and cherry amplify on the finish, but it avoids disaster by keeping the acidity bright and tannins usefully employed. Zinfandel devotees will feel immediately at home, and this is hardly a coincidence: Primitivo and Zinfandel are distant cousins, explaining their common boldness and capacity for density. B+ / $34

title: Review: Rabbit Hole Raceking Bourbon (2026)
summary:

The original Raceking was a limited edition offering that was part of Rabbit Hole’s Founder’s Collection series, but now it’s gone more mainstream, featuring the same five-grain mashbill featuring chocolate-malted wheat and chocolate-malted…

The post Review: Rabbit Hole Raceking Bourbon (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Don’t get tripped up: The Raceking of today is connected to the Raceking of the past, but it’s not the same thing. The original Raceking was a limited edition offering that was part of Rabbit Hole’s Founder’s Collection series, but now it’s gone more mainstream, featuring the same five-grain mashbill featuring chocolate-malted wheat and chocolate-malted barley, an (older) 6 year old age statement, and a lower, standardized proof.

“Raceking reflects how I like to approach bourbon, with respect for tradition but a willingness to explore its edges,” said Kaveh Zamanian, founder of Rabbit Hole Distillery. “With this release, we wanted to honor Kentucky’s legendary horse racing tradition. The name Raceking reflects that heritage and embodies the careful, deliberate process required to craft a bourbon worthy of a thoroughbred pedigree. Every element, from our five-grain mash bill to the toasted and charred barrels, was designed to create a bold, distinct flavor that celebrates both Kentucky’s history and Rabbit Hole’s approach to thoughtful whiskey making.”

With the cask strength designation dropped, Raceking’s price has also plummeted, from an MSRP of $395 to just $95 for the new edition.

We covered two editions of the Founder’s Collection bottling, most recently in 2023. Now we’re ready to see how the people’s Raceking compares.

Rabbit Hole Raceking Bourbon (2026) Review

The incorporation of two chocolate-malted grains is no joke, and straight from the bottle, Raceking smells just like you opened the door of a chocolate factory. The intense aroma of cocoa powder blows off a bit after a moment, making room for cinnamon and some gentle notes of wood shavings. It’s all well-integrated into that pastry shop attack, a chocolate croissant, freshly baked.

All of these carry through to the palate, though it surprised me as coming across as slightly boozy and youngish, with some undercooked cereal elements in the mix. These are short-lived, however, and soon enough the more exuberant elements of the whiskey take over again. As Drew has mentioned in previous reviews of the old Raceking, coffee bean is a clear component on the tongue, along with some dark cherry fruitiness. There’s an ample wood influence in the mix, but it’s well-integrated into the experience. The only real shift I can see here is the lack of any smoky qualities, which could well be driven by the choice to bottle this at a lower abv.

Ultimately, this feels like you’re getting the full Raceking experience of yesteryear, and I have to think you probably won’t miss the reduction in proof. The $300 you’ll save on a bottle — that you’ll notice.

95 proof.

A- / $95

title: Review: Bota Box Cabernet Sauvignon, Nighthawk Bourbon Barrel Aged Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon
summary:
Are people ready to give boxed wine a fair shake? I hope so, because they actually have a lot to recommend them. Today we are trying three boxed cabernet sauvignons from Bota Box. All three are very reasonably priced and come in a box that is recyclable, made primarily from renewable, plant-based materials, and produces…

The post Review: Bota Box Cabernet Sauvignon, Nighthawk Bourbon Barrel Aged Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Are people ready to give boxed wine a fair shake? I hope so, because they actually have a lot to recommend them. Today we are trying three boxed cabernet sauvignons from Bota Box. All three are very reasonably priced and come in a box that is recyclable, made primarily from renewable, plant-based materials, and produces less solid waste and a smaller carbon footprint than glass bottles. The boxes typically hold the equivalent of two or four bottles of wine, but because the wine container is airtight, the wine will stay good for up to 30 days, so there is no rush to finish it before oxidation kicks in. Growing respect for boxed wine is starting to encourage companies to sell better quality wines in boxes, and today we will be trying Bota Box’s various cabernet sauvignon offerings. Let’s tap some boxes and give these wines a try.

Bota Box Cabernet Sauvignon – On both the nose and palate, there’s jammy black cherry, blackberry, light black pepper, and a touch of band-aid. That last note is a bit unpleasant, but happily, it is only a touch, and the fruity notes play a much larger role in the wine’s character. The wine shows medium acidity and a touch of drying tannic structure on the finish. At this price point, you can’t expect much more, and I am happy to find it here. For the price, this is a decent wine, and it would be perfect to bring on a camping trip to enjoy on a cold night under the stars. B- / $18 for 3L box

Bota Box Nighthawk Bourbon Barrel Aged Cabernet Sauvignon – Enjoyable dark fruit notes of blackberry and blueberry along with a touch of vanilla and a little alcohol emerge from the glass. The palate follows the nose nicely with lightly boozy blackberry and blueberry, rounded with a touch of vanilla and a bit of milk chocolate. The bourbon barrel aging brings a lot to the wine, rounding it off but without imposing a strong bourbon note. The medium acidity integrates well with the fruit, and the tannins show up in the finish with a drying touch. I was impressed. B / $18 for 3L box

Bota Box Limited Reserve Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon – So let’s answer the big question first: Does it taste like a true Napa Valley cabernet? Well, kinda. On the nose and palate, enjoyable notes of plum, cassis, and raspberry emerge, and a touch of milk chocolate appears in the background. The tannins are light, but they’re there, providing a bit of a drying finish, and the acidity is low to medium. I’d have loved to see more structure and bolder, more clarified flavors, but let’s keep things in perspective: This is a very nice glass of wine at a fantastic price. It does not come close to the great wines from the region but it deserves a place of respect for the quality it brings at an affordable price. If I’m making steaks or even burgers for a big group of friends, I wouldn’t hesitate to get a box or two to pair with them. B+ / $20 for 1.5L box

title: Review: Old Forester Birthday Bourbon 2026 Edition
summary:
212 barrels drawn from the third floor of Warehouse B, the oldest warehouse at the Brown-Forman Distillery in Shively, went into the production of Old Forester’s 2026 Birthday Bourbon. With Master Distiller Emeritus Chris Morris and Assistant Master Distiller Caleb Trigo behind the scenes, it’s an 11 year old expression that, as always, helps us…

The post Review: Old Forester Birthday Bourbon 2026 Edition appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
212 barrels drawn from the third floor of Warehouse B, the oldest warehouse at the Brown-Forman Distillery in Shively, went into the production of Old Forester’s 2026 Birthday Bourbon. With Master Distiller Emeritus Chris Morris and Assistant Master Distiller Caleb Trigo behind the scenes, it’s an 11 year old expression that, as always, helps us to commemorate the beginning of whiskey season, a time marked by the year’s most prized whiskey drops, which will stretch from now until the end of the year.

We were fortunate to score a sample of this year’s offering to put it to the test.

Old Forester Birthday Bourbon 2026 Edition Review

Of all the big annual whiskey releases, Old Fo’s Birthday Bourbon is the one that can be the most hit-and-miss, but this year the distillery has produced a real — if slightly unorthodox — delight.

The nose tells the story in broad strokes: A curious coconut note starts things off, followed by a heavily toasted bread quality. Baking spice is present, but quite muted, ceding time for ample brown butter to appear, a natural complement that turns a bit scorched as it develops in glass. By the end, barrel char becomes dominant, though the more exotic elements maintain some influence — particularly that coconut, along with a bit of brown banana.

The palate is sweet and creamy, those banana notes becoming a bit riper and brighter on the tongue, the coconut evocative of a chocolate-coconut cream pie. A lively cherry note comes into focus after the initial rush of flavor fades, making for a surprisingly satisfying counterpoint to the increasingly wood-forward nose. The combined sweet-and-savory quality never feels standard-issue, and it gives the whiskey a ton of depth, almost lip-smackingly inviting, particularly at a wholly approachable 97 proof.

There’s a reprise of wood and some black pepper, then dried mint, on the modest but satisfying finish. It’s quite a little ride, quirky and unconventional in its own way, but a special installment in a long-running series that deserves to be discovered. So, what are you waiting for?

97 proof.

A / $200 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: Three Ships 6 Years Old Chenin Blanc Cask appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
South Africa’s James Sedgwick Distillery is no stranger to experimental cask finishing, and given Chenin Blanc is the country’s most widely-planted grape varietal, it was only a matter of time before someone paired these casks with a whisky to represent something uniquely South African.

Released as the seventh addition to the Three Ships Master’s Collection, this whisky is produced from column-distilled malt and aged in American oak casks of varying ages before resting in Chenin Blanc wine casks for two years.

Three Ships 6 Years Old Chenin Blanc Cask Review

The nose is bright, inviting, and strikes a beautiful balance between spirit and cask. Initially it
offers a typical bourbon cask signature, while the wine cask’s fingerprint takes a little longer
to settle. The balance of oak, malt sweetness, and vanilla, blended with the excitement of
lemon zest, peach, and grapefruit, makes for an enjoyable aromatic experience. There’s also
a perfumed note present on the nose which blends well between the fruit and oak aromas,
however, some may find it unpleasant.

On the palate, the Chenin Blanc cask finish is more evident. It hits with sweet honey and
vanilla upfront, followed by vibrant pineapple, pear, apple, and a bright citrus tang to cut
through the body and carries through to the finish. Ginger builds gradually, adding structure
rather than heat. The finish leaves behind orchard fruit, soft spice, drying oak, and a slight
minerality.

What is most impressive about this whisky is its balance. It’s easy for a wine cask to steal
some spotlight from the spirit. However, here the Chenin Blanc casks brighten the
whisky’s profile, enhancing freshness while maintaining the character of the spirit. This
finish feels purposeful rather than experimental, and this one is easily one of my favorite
wine cask finishes.

This expression reinforces Three Ships’ reputation as a leading brand of South African
whisky. This edition is distinctive without chasing novelty and offers incredible value for
money. It’s available for around $45 and should appeal to whisky enthusiasts looking for
something beyond sherry and Port finishes, or perhaps an everyday summer dram.

86 proof.

B+ / $45

title: Review: First West Explorer Bourbon
summary:
Once bottled as part of the 15 Stars empire, First West just spun itself out into its own brand (though “crafted by 15 Stars” still appears on the label in small print), complete with different branding and a weird-looking bottle that reminds me of a fish. (Turns out these are also historically inspired by the…

The post Review: First West Explorer Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Once bottled as part of the 15 Stars empire, First West just spun itself out into its own brand (though “crafted by 15 Stars” still appears on the label in small print), complete with different branding and a weird-looking bottle that reminds me of a fish. (Turns out these are also historically inspired by the bottles of yore.)

While the corporate branding is its own — First West being a reference to how Kentucky was the first stop on the westward expansion into the frontier — the production process is really the same: Like 15 Stars, these are sourced Kentucky whiskeys, at least for the most part. The brand now contains four expressions, of which we received one: Explorer. With Explorer, its a four-grain blend of 15 Stars’ own distillate — two mashbills, both 5 years old or more, one of which includes black corn on the mash. While unclear to me initially, this is the first release from 15 Stars to be comprised completely of the company’s own distillate. (Thanks to Eric T. for clarifying all of this; see comments below for more detail.)

Let’s taste it.

First West Explorer Bourbon Review

After a somewhat brash attack on the nose, Explorer manages to air itself out a bit and tame what feels like a bit of a beast. Unfortunately, what’s left behind is a little scattered — butterscotch and caramel corn, quite sweet, backed up by lumberyard and black pepper aromas, some earthy greenery ringing the edges.

The palate is a contrast: All corn, or nearly all corn, anyway. Here the caramel corn finds loads of fresh-popped popcorn folded in, first coming across as quite savory before the whiskey’s natural sweetness grows anew and evolves further into candied territory, evoking peanut brittle dipped in cinnamon syrup. The midpalate is otherwise indistinct, showing a bit of mint and some cherry Sucrets notes, before a somewhat short, slightly underdeveloped conclusion. Ultimately this winds up as one of those whiskeys that feels mostly harmless and otherwise indistinct, though nothing at which I’d turn my nose up at happy hour.

95 proof.

B / $50

title: Review: Woodford Reserve Master’s Collection Super Seasoned Oak Bourbon
summary:
Woodford Reserve‘s 22nd installment of its beloved Master’s Collection is upon us, and while these experimental releases can be out-there, this 2026 expression is something quite unusual. Super Seasoned Oak has nothing to do with spice or pepper but rather refers to the practice of “seasoning” newly milled barrel staves by letting them dry in…

The post Review: Woodford Reserve Master’s Collection Super Seasoned Oak Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Woodford Reserve‘s 22nd installment of its beloved Master’s Collection is upon us, and while these experimental releases can be out-there, this 2026 expression is something quite unusual. Super Seasoned Oak has nothing to do with spice or pepper but rather refers to the practice of “seasoning” newly milled barrel staves by letting them dry in the open air before they are used to create casks. (The process reduces harsh tannins and allows tight wood grain to open up, allowing liquid to seep into it.) Traditional oak staves must be seasoned for a year or two before they are put to use in barrel construction. With Super Seasoned Oak, those staves spend between five and seven years drying before being turned into barrels.

Surprisingly, there’s no additional information about the actual whiskey that was aged in these barrels, but it’s safe to say it’s the standard Woodford bourbon recipe, aged for roughly the same amount of time as the standby.

Woodford Reserve Master’s Collection Super Seasoned Oak Bourbon Review

The results here are solid, and quite surprising. While I would suspect there are diminishing returns to be gained after the first few years of leaving wood outside to dry, it turns out the excessive drying time coaxes out plenty of sugar from the wood… which ends up in the whiskey.

The nose is at first familiar (though not wholly Woodfordian), with an ample, peanutty sweetness that hits heavy from the start. Vanilla is dominant, with notes of maple adding even more sweetness to the aroma. Fruit picks up from there (primarily raisin), but it can be a little slow going, with a traditional barrel char note lingering over the proceedings. All told, that sweet vanilla-driven syrupiness makes for a decidedly dessert-like attack that sets the stage for the experience to come.

The palate does not let off the gas. This is a very sweet whiskey, that peanut character emerging as candied brittle, laced more clearly with maple and some raisin notes. Heavy cinnamon notes build significantly, layering with tons of vanilla to create a creamy flavor that would be perfectly at home as a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream flavor. The spicy richness clings to every corner of the mouth, layers of increasingly dark, dried berries dripping over the top of the bourbon. A raisin/prune character lingers on the finish, injected heavily with baking spice and, as it sits in glass, a bit of hoary creosote that sees some tannic funk creeping in.

To be frank, I was not expecting this level of sweetness from the whiskey — particularly given that it’s a Woodford product — and ultimately I found it a bit much to handle. While it’s very instructive in showcasing what excessive wood seasoning can do to a whiskey, it’s not particularly balanced, making it more useful as a proof of concept rather than a full-scale sipper.

100.4 proof.

B+ / $180

title: Review: 2025 Harken Chardonnay California
summary:
The ABC (Anything but Chardonnay) movement didn’t really take hold the way some people would have hoped. All of its most boisterous vocal proponents either set off to the great big vineyard in the sky or moved on to putting Merlot or Rosé on blast. But certain Chardonnays are serving as proof of victory, and…

The post Review: 2025 Harken Chardonnay California appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The ABC (Anything but Chardonnay) movement didn’t really take hold the way some people would have hoped. All of its most boisterous vocal proponents either set off to the great big vineyard in the sky or moved on to putting Merlot or Rosé on blast. But certain Chardonnays are serving as proof of victory, and Harken’s Chardonnay is one of them. Like most eccentric Californians, they are fully committed to the bit of doing one thing well and are wholly unbothered by media trends. Harken simply does Chardonnay and that’s that.

The nose opens with an expected roll call of citrus: orange, lemon, and pear, eventually followed by vanilla from oak aging arriving just a few beats behind. On the palate, pear carries through, joined by roasted nuts and a rich, custardy quality reminiscent of crème brulèe. This isn’t a lean, mineral-driven Chardonnay by any stretch, and it leans fully into a rich sweetness. The finish is long and citrus-forward, with a thin thread of minerality appearing late that provides balance and contrast against the buttery, oak-driven weight of everything that came before.

This is a classic old-school California Chardonnay. The kind people either adore or pretend to have grown out of during social gatherings. It’s also an unquestionably genuine bargain, making it feel less of a guilty pleasure and more like a good call for the bank balance. Crack it open in late October or early November, paired with roasted root vegetables, and let it do what it’s been aiming to do: strut its stuff with pride.

B+ / $16

title: Review: Redwood Empire The Hyperion
summary:
Bay Area, California-based Redwood Empire recently dropped a new limited edition offering dubbed “The Hyperion,” named after the world’s tallest living tree in California’s Redwood National Park, which it calls its most ambitious project yet. What’s in the bottle? A little bit of everything. Creating “The Hyperion” Batch 001 began, intentionally, without an established path.…

The post Review: Redwood Empire The Hyperion appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Bay Area, California-based Redwood Empire recently dropped a new limited edition offering dubbed “The Hyperion,” named after the world’s tallest living tree in California’s Redwood National Park, which it calls its most ambitious project yet. What’s in the bottle? A little bit of everything.

Creating “The Hyperion” Batch 001 began, intentionally, without an established path. Redwood Empire’s Master Distiller-Master Blender duo explored a broad terrain of mature barrels, crossing the traditional boundaries separating bourbon, rye, wheat whiskey, and single malt whiskey. The resulting 110-proof expression brings together four distinct whiskey categories, more than 10 mashbills, and stocks aged from 7 to 14 years, arriving at a destination no single whiskey could reach on its own.

“The Hyperion is an exercise in artistry. Regal, refined, bold. A collaboration of spirit types that fully brings to light the depth and diversity of our barrel inventory,” said Lauren Patz, Master Blender at Redwood Empire Whiskey. “Wheat Whiskey, Bourbon, Rye, and American Single Malt find both balance and transformation and demonstrate what can emerge when curiosity is matched with patience and purpose.”

In lieu of a traditional mash bill, the inaugural label instead boasts a blend bill—a collection of whiskey blends, rather than simply mashes—of 32% bourbon whiskey, 30% rye whiskey, 25% wheat whiskey, and 13% single malt whiskey. The final blend of approximately 79 barrels combines multiple mash bills from curated whiskey stocks from Redwood Empire and other distillers in Indiana, Kentucky, and Tennessee. Each category combines multiple mash bills from a total of 50-100 barrels of curated whiskey stocks from Redwood Empire and others distilled in Indiana, Kentucky, and Tennessee. The single malt component is entirely grain-to-glass whiskey distilled by Redwood Empire. The blended whiskey entered the barrel between 110 and 120 proof and matured in toasted, Char No. 3 barrels. Maturation takes place in Northern California, where warm days give way to fog-laced cool winds off the Pacific at night.

Whoa.

Also dig the wooden bottle stopper, another unique and very cool touch to cap off an interesting spirit.

Redwood Empire The Hyperion Review

The whiskey noses with the expected complexity, but sweetness dominates. Vanilla syrup, short of cake frosting but getting there, meanders toward chocolate syrup, raspberry glaze, and a stone fruit compote. Increasingly spicy and nutty as it gets a bit of air, the whiskey’s buttery core never loses any steam at all.

The palate finds many of the same elements but ups the ante further. Sweet and buttery, it drinks like well-slathered cinnamon toast, almost syrupy in texture at times. Coconut is dominant on the midpalate, again creamy to the point where it feels like it could fit in in a pina colada. This lingers for ages before segueing toward milk chocolate, caramel, and toffee notes, with touches of brown banana creating something of a banana split character. Dollops of whipped cream top things off.

All told, this is a far sunnier and sweeter whiskey than I was expecting, perhaps unexpectedly driven by the wheat whiskey in the blend. I’m not mad at it.

Reviewed: Batch 1. 110 proof.

A- / $99

title: Tasting Report: Malbecs for Fall 2026
summary:
Every declining empire eventually presents the same magic trick: debase the currency while publicly insisting it has never held higher value and reverence. American wine pricing has absorbed the lesson well. Malbec, a grape spending most of its history as a humble tenant in the cellars of the working class, continues to experience inflation normally…

The post Tasting Report: Malbecs for Fall 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Every declining empire eventually presents the same magic trick: debase the currency while publicly insisting it has never held higher value and reverence. American wine pricing has absorbed the lesson well. Malbec, a grape spending most of its history as a humble tenant in the cellars of the working class, continues to experience inflation normally reserved for the 100-point Parkeratti of Wine. Bottles once asking a reasonable price now demand tribute. Prestige labels, the aristocracy of any bull market, have taken to pricing themselves like sovereign debt.

Somehow, supply multiplies in obedience to demand, as it always does in the final stages of any speculative romance. What inflation has purchased, at least, are certain improvements. Ambitious producers are rewarded and quality continues to elevate. The conversation around Malbec is no longer the exclusive property of France and Argentina but can now also be claimed by domestic upstarts minting their own currency. Thankfully, good value can still be found by those willing to audit the books.

Now in its second year, we present an autumnal audit of recent Malbecs, from everyday considerations to the ostensibly cellar-worthy, in preparation for cold months and potentially even colder experiences with relatives during the holidays.

2025 Mendoza Vineyards Heroes Malbec Lujan de Cuyo – Created in tribute to the Argentina Men’s National Team for the 2026 World Cup. Unlike that team, this offering does not fall short of expectations: cherry, dark chocolate and coal running throughout, with herbs and a bit of soil eventually cutting through. Also unlike that team, this has a classy finish which lingers nicely and doesn’t attempt to start fights after the final whistle. One to pick up if you’re still in mourning, or cellar for the next four years. There’s always hope things will get better from here.  A- / $50

2021 Nico Malbec Gualtallary – Not to be confused with the Nico line produced by Luca (I know). Another year brings yet another expression to the expansive portfolio of Laura Catena and crew. Deep notes of raspberry and cherry run throughout, along with layers of blueberry, thyme, cassis and a touch of menthol. Nothing here really stands out and everyone plays together nicely. Traces of cedar plank also appear on the finish, allowing savory elements to amplify. It needs a bit of time and air, but once this finds its footing, it’s a wine that will endear itself to the most devoted Malbec mavens. Stacks up against its siblings commanding double the price, and one to open during a celebration in the cooler months. Quite lovely.  A / $120

2024 Zuccardi Concreto Malbec Valle du Uco – Without the reliance of oak barrel aging, this Zuccardi skips the dark fruit jam session and showcases herbaceous and mineral notes on the nose. The dark fruit eventually comes into focus on the palate, full of juicy plum and raspberry. However, that minerality returns in a big way on the finish. It’s a lively Malbec just slightly off the beaten path, and shows just how versatile and beautiful Malbec can be in the hands of a competence.  A- / $45

2020 Château de Mercuès Les Evêques Malbec Cahors – The brooding quality and boldness of this Vigouroux offering is usually reserved for the heaviest of Mendoza malbecs, and not something one would normally expect from the French. Blackberry, plum and Lapsang tea form a dense core that runs throughout, with a palate that recedes ever so slightly with an appearance of dark cherry on the palate and a finish providing a tinge of campfire smoke. Drink now if your curiosity gets the best of you, but allow for an adequate amount of time before serving. Otherwise, keep this around for 2028.  A- / $35

2022 Illaria Malbec Napa Valley – A Malbec-Cabernet Sauvignon blend of 84% and 16%, respectively. Initially dense with blackberry and blueberry, it eventually opens up with layers of dark chocolate, raspberry and rosemary. The oak pulls its weight on the finish, with touches of vanilla, graphite pencil and minerality lingering. This has aged 22 months in the barrel, and would likely do well with an equal measure of time in the cellar. B+ / $50

2023 Trivento Golden Reserve Malbec Lujan de Cuyo – There is a familiar and appealing medley immediately present that Malbec fans will appreciate: big notes of cherry and plum with cola, blackberry and chocolate all making appearances over time. Moderate acidity and tannins give this a good structure and make it a sensible weeknight pairing with a quick and easy meal off the grill to show off some of its charms. Still consistent and an excellent value purchase. For now. B+ / $20

2025 Domaine Bousquet Reserve Organic Malbec – Domaine Bousquet has made some branding changes over the years to their expansive lineup, so it may be hard to tell what is what without looking closely. However, this one stays the same and is all the better for it: dark fruit, baking spice and cedar work their way to a palate big on berries and earthy notes. The good acidity keeps matters from turning too beefy, and the floral lift keeps it easy drinking. A dependable release that hasn’t really increased in price over the years. Picking up one to age, one to have on hand to entertain uninvited house guests and one for now isn’t the worst idea.  B+ / $22

2024 Waterbrook Malbec Columbia Valley – Sometimes Malbec can show up being big, purple-faced and loud: the equivalent of a sweat-drenched guy who chicken-struts off the dance floor at a wedding to scream-explain cryptocurrency to everyone within earshot at the open bar. Westbrook doesn’t do this. It shows up lighter-bodied but still comes fully stocked with personality and restraint. Opening aromas of raspberry compote and blueberry threaten to make this a fruit bomb. But the threat is diffused on the palate, where darker tones of blackberry and black tea meld with violet and dark chocolate amidst good acidity and gentle tannins. A rare find of quality and affordability in a domestic market that leans overblown and inflated.  B+ / $20

2022 L’Atelier Crocus Malbec Cahors – A collaboration between Paul Hobbs and Gabriel Vigouroux. Intense blackcurrant supported by strawberry makes for a less-than-silent introduction, with notes of black pepper and plum as it winds its way to the finish, where a mild touch of chocolate settles things down nicely. Give this a year or so tucked away somewhere and the dividend will pay off.  B / $22

2023 OG de Négoce Lot 518 Napa Valley Malbec – I got this wrong. I was hoping that a year or so tucked away would yield improved results. It did not. This Napa Valley interpretation of a traditional Mendoza Malbec didn’t really move the needle in a positive direction, and it the dark fruit compote still dominates over all else. It’s a perfectly serviceable bottle, but it doesn’t really stand out in the crowd the way something from Napa ought to.  B / $22

2023 Trivento White Malbec Mendoza – Affordable and slightly unassuming, notes of white flower and herbs are evident at the start. However, with a bit of time, the wine develops more dimension to reveal a citrus edge of guava and hints of mango. It’s approachable and quite youthful, and one to have around that is more of a curiosity than a go-to.  B- / $13

2024 La Posta Pizzella Malbec Mendoza – A perennial everyday Malbec staple for years in our house, this year’s vintage failed to meet the standard. The hallmark raspberry and violet notes on the nose are still there, as is the plum, pepper and spice on the palate. But it never seems to really sort itself out and results in a jammy, overbearing affair. If possible, seek out older vintages.  C / $18

2025 Be Calm Malbec Argentina – All the usual suspects are present and accounted for: blackberry, plum, cinnamon, pepper and pencil shavings. However, it is so watered down that it becomes a laborious, sometimes painful, chore to even slow sip this. Best served in a chilled glass. Then, calmly, pour that glass straight down the drain immediately, muttering a silent apology to the drainage pipes.  D / $10

The post Tasting Report: Malbecs for Fall 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.

title: Review: Parker’s Heritage Collection Kentucky Straight Bourbon with Rye Backset 14 Years Old (2026)
summary:
The 20th edition of Heaven Hill Distillery’s Parker’s Heritage Collection Limited Edition bottling reads a bit strangely on paper, but I promise it’s easier than the convoluted name suggests. First, the broad technical details: Comprised of 100 barrels, the 20th Edition is made from Heaven Hill’s traditional Bourbon mashbill of 78% corn, 10% rye and…

The post Review: Parker’s Heritage Collection Kentucky Straight Bourbon with Rye Backset 14 Years Old (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The 20th edition of Heaven Hill Distillery’s Parker’s Heritage Collection Limited Edition bottling reads a bit strangely on paper, but I promise it’s easier than the convoluted name suggests.

First, the broad technical details:

Comprised of 100 barrels, the 20th Edition is made from Heaven Hill’s traditional Bourbon mashbill of 78% corn, 10% rye and 12% malted barley. Distilled between October 2011 and January 2012, the whiskey was aged for 14 years across four rickhouses and multiple floors: Rickhouse A on the second floor; Rickhouse KK on the first and second floors; and Rickhouses L and M on the third floor.

The twist comes with the bit about the “rye backset,” which refers to the portion of the liquid left after a distillation run that is traditionally reused in the next batch to improve consistency of flavor from batch to batch. Here, the backset used is rye whiskey, not bourbon, which was one of Parker Beam’s signature moves. It’s uncommon today, however, which makes this release particularly intriguing.

“Parker understood that the smallest details in the whiskey making process can have a meaningful impact on the final pour,” said Conor O’Driscoll, Heaven Hill Master Distiller. “This edition reflects that belief, using rye backset to create a 14-year-old Bourbon with remarkable depth, balance and spice. We’re proud to honor Parker’s enduring influence through a release that celebrates his steadfast belief in making the highest quality whiskey.”

As always, a portion of proceeds support the ALS Association, the disease with which Beam was diagnosed in 2010 and ultimately perished from.

I’m ready to tuck in to Parker’s Heritage XX. Here goes.

Parker’s Heritage Collection Kentucky Straight Bourbon with Rye Backset 14 Years Old (2026) Review

Let’s be frank: A rye backset means there’s more than a little rye in the finished product here, and it’s awfully hard to miss. Spice of both the baking and savory variety is heavy on the nose, though the aroma is also quite sweet, evoking elements of tangerine juice, fresh honey, and sweet tea. It’s a little tight at first blush (at 59% abv, that’s understandable), and a healthy splash of water helps decode the nose a bit more clearly, turning out more traditional notes of vanilla and milk chocolate.

The palate’s sweetness is immediate and, even given the foreshadowing of the nose, a little surprising. Golden syrup, touched with citrus, mixed florals, and vanilla custard are all dominant, with cinnamon-heavy spice building as the midpalate takes hold. This mixes with a latent barrel char quality that adds some back-of-palate grittiness to the experience, and while it isn’t overbearing, it does stick with you, coating the throat with a red pepper urgency.

Time in glass (and more water) help coax out more nuance. That black tea segues into green tea, with notes of tobacco becoming more forceful on the surprisingly pushy, lengthy finish.

I spent a long while noodling over this whiskey, which is entirely engaging and always enjoyable, but which felt like it might be struggling to tell its story with complete coherence. The punch of rye spice is more than evident, but there’s so much exuberant sweetness to balance it out that neither side of the equation ever completely takes over. Perhaps it was pulled a few years too early? That’s something I rarely say at the double-digit age level.

This is a whiskey that has been clinging to me for hours, long after I’ve washed my Glencairn. Part of me is still processing.

118 proof.

A- / $200

title: Review: Varvaglione 2023 Susumaniello Rosso Puglia and 2022 Papale Primitivo di Manduria DOP Linea Oro
summary:
A regional pride emerges in places the rest of the wine world spent a century overlooking on the way to somewhere more famous. Puglia (Apulia) is one of those areas. It stands as the bottom of Italy’s boot, doing the unglamorous work of growing things sun-baked and historically responsible for supplying the country’s bulk wine…

The post Review: Varvaglione 2023 Susumaniello Rosso Puglia and 2022 Papale Primitivo di Manduria DOP Linea Oro appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
A regional pride emerges in places the rest of the wine world spent a century overlooking on the way to somewhere more famous. Puglia (Apulia) is one of those areas. It stands as the bottom of Italy’s boot, doing the unglamorous work of growing things sun-baked and historically responsible for supplying the country’s bulk wine needs while Tuscany and Piedmont earned the magazine covers. Salento, the heel of that boot, is where the Varvaglione family set up shop in 1921. The founding myth here is modest: a guy named Cosimo, some vines outside Pulsano, and no particular ambition beyond keeping his own household in wine. Word got out, and it wasn’t long before sailors stationed at the nearby naval base were knocking on his door, which is its own kind of five-star review: nothing moves bottles quite like a fleet of bored, off-duty people in the military. One century and four generations later, the operation has grown considerably, but it hasn’t drifted. Today, we check in with two of their flagship offerings.

2023 Varvaglione Susumaniello Rosso Puglia – Quite dense and full-bodied, this wine heavily front-loads spice and balsamic and leans heavily into savory, earthy notes of mushroom and black pepper with time in the glass. Strawberry and black cherry come into focus on the palate as it develops, balancing the savory qualities that push so heavily up front. The finish is unwilling to go lightly, and revisits the balsamic thesis, accompanied by a coda of cocoa powder and black cherry. This is not a wine for idle company or light fare: it’s brooding and needs to be served with something substantial. B+ / $27

2022 Varvaglione Papale Primitivo di Manduria DOP Linea Oro – This 100% Primitivo di Manduria is an intense blend of rhubarb, cherry compote and tobacco leaf straight through, with orange zest and raspberry making intermittent appearances on the palate. The rhubarb and cherry amplify on the finish, but it avoids disaster by keeping the acidity bright and tannins usefully employed. Zinfandel devotees will feel immediately at home, and this is hardly a coincidence: Primitivo and Zinfandel are distant cousins, explaining their common boldness and capacity for density. B+ / $34

title: Review: Rabbit Hole Raceking Bourbon (2026)
summary:
Don’t get tripped up: The Raceking of today is connected to the Raceking of the past, but it’s not the same thing. The original Raceking was a limited edition offering that was part of Rabbit Hole’s Founder’s Collection series, but now it’s gone more mainstream, featuring the same five-grain mashbill featuring chocolate-malted wheat and chocolate-malted…

The post Review: Rabbit Hole Raceking Bourbon (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Don’t get tripped up: The Raceking of today is connected to the Raceking of the past, but it’s not the same thing. The original Raceking was a limited edition offering that was part of Rabbit Hole’s Founder’s Collection series, but now it’s gone more mainstream, featuring the same five-grain mashbill featuring chocolate-malted wheat and chocolate-malted barley, an (older) 6 year old age statement, and a lower, standardized proof.

“Raceking reflects how I like to approach bourbon, with respect for tradition but a willingness to explore its edges,” said Kaveh Zamanian, founder of Rabbit Hole Distillery. “With this release, we wanted to honor Kentucky’s legendary horse racing tradition. The name Raceking reflects that heritage and embodies the careful, deliberate process required to craft a bourbon worthy of a thoroughbred pedigree. Every element, from our five-grain mash bill to the toasted and charred barrels, was designed to create a bold, distinct flavor that celebrates both Kentucky’s history and Rabbit Hole’s approach to thoughtful whiskey making.”

With the cask strength designation dropped, Raceking’s price has also plummeted, from an MSRP of $395 to just $95 for the new edition.

We covered two editions of the Founder’s Collection bottling, most recently in 2023. Now we’re ready to see how the people’s Raceking compares.

Rabbit Hole Raceking Bourbon (2026) Review

The incorporation of two chocolate-malted grains is no joke, and straight from the bottle, Raceking smells just like you opened the door of a chocolate factory. The intense aroma of cocoa powder blows off a bit after a moment, making room for cinnamon and some gentle notes of wood shavings. It’s all well-integrated into that pastry shop attack, a chocolate croissant, freshly baked.

All of these carry through to the palate, though it surprised me as coming across as slightly boozy and youngish, with some undercooked cereal elements in the mix. These are short-lived, however, and soon enough the more exuberant elements of the whiskey take over again. As Drew has mentioned in previous reviews of the old Raceking, coffee bean is a clear component on the tongue, along with some dark cherry fruitiness. There’s an ample wood influence in the mix, but it’s well-integrated into the experience. The only real shift I can see here is the lack of any smoky qualities, which could well be driven by the choice to bottle this at a lower abv.

Ultimately, this feels like you’re getting the full Raceking experience of yesteryear, and I have to think you probably won’t miss the reduction in proof. The $300 you’ll save on a bottle — that you’ll notice.

95 proof.

A- / $95

summary:
Are people ready to give boxed wine a fair shake? I hope so, because they actually have a lot to recommend them. Today we are trying three boxed cabernet sauvignons from Bota Box. All three are very reasonably priced and come in a box that is recyclable, made primarily from renewable, plant-based materials, and produces…

The post Review: Bota Box Cabernet Sauvignon, Nighthawk Bourbon Barrel Aged Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Are people ready to give boxed wine a fair shake? I hope so, because they actually have a lot to recommend them. Today we are trying three boxed cabernet sauvignons from Bota Box. All three are very reasonably priced and come in a box that is recyclable, made primarily from renewable, plant-based materials, and produces less solid waste and a smaller carbon footprint than glass bottles. The boxes typically hold the equivalent of two or four bottles of wine, but because the wine container is airtight, the wine will stay good for up to 30 days, so there is no rush to finish it before oxidation kicks in. Growing respect for boxed wine is starting to encourage companies to sell better quality wines in boxes, and today we will be trying Bota Box’s various cabernet sauvignon offerings. Let’s tap some boxes and give these wines a try.

Bota Box Cabernet Sauvignon – On both the nose and palate, there’s jammy black cherry, blackberry, light black pepper, and a touch of band-aid. That last note is a bit unpleasant, but happily, it is only a touch, and the fruity notes play a much larger role in the wine’s character. The wine shows medium acidity and a touch of drying tannic structure on the finish. At this price point, you can’t expect much more, and I am happy to find it here. For the price, this is a decent wine, and it would be perfect to bring on a camping trip to enjoy on a cold night under the stars. B- / $18 for 3L box

Bota Box Nighthawk Bourbon Barrel Aged Cabernet Sauvignon – Enjoyable dark fruit notes of blackberry and blueberry along with a touch of vanilla and a little alcohol emerge from the glass. The palate follows the nose nicely with lightly boozy blackberry and blueberry, rounded with a touch of vanilla and a bit of milk chocolate. The bourbon barrel aging brings a lot to the wine, rounding it off but without imposing a strong bourbon note. The medium acidity integrates well with the fruit, and the tannins show up in the finish with a drying touch. I was impressed. B / $18 for 3L box

Bota Box Limited Reserve Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon – So let’s answer the big question first: Does it taste like a true Napa Valley cabernet? Well, kinda. On the nose and palate, enjoyable notes of plum, cassis, and raspberry emerge, and a touch of milk chocolate appears in the background. The tannins are light, but they’re there, providing a bit of a drying finish, and the acidity is low to medium. I’d have loved to see more structure and bolder, more clarified flavors, but let’s keep things in perspective: This is a very nice glass of wine at a fantastic price. It does not come close to the great wines from the region but it deserves a place of respect for the quality it brings at an affordable price. If I’m making steaks or even burgers for a big group of friends, I wouldn’t hesitate to get a box or two to pair with them. B+ / $20 for 1.5L box

The post Review: Old Forester Birthday Bourbon 2026 Edition appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
212 barrels drawn from the third floor of Warehouse B, the oldest warehouse at the Brown-Forman Distillery in Shively, went into the production of Old Forester’s 2026 Birthday Bourbon. With Master Distiller Emeritus Chris Morris and Assistant Master Distiller Caleb Trigo behind the scenes, it’s an 11 year old expression that, as always, helps us to commemorate the beginning of whiskey season, a time marked by the year’s most prized whiskey drops, which will stretch from now until the end of the year.

We were fortunate to score a sample of this year’s offering to put it to the test.

Old Forester Birthday Bourbon 2026 Edition Review

Of all the big annual whiskey releases, Old Fo’s Birthday Bourbon is the one that can be the most hit-and-miss, but this year the distillery has produced a real — if slightly unorthodox — delight.

The nose tells the story in broad strokes: A curious coconut note starts things off, followed by a heavily toasted bread quality. Baking spice is present, but quite muted, ceding time for ample brown butter to appear, a natural complement that turns a bit scorched as it develops in glass. By the end, barrel char becomes dominant, though the more exotic elements maintain some influence — particularly that coconut, along with a bit of brown banana.

The palate is sweet and creamy, those banana notes becoming a bit riper and brighter on the tongue, the coconut evocative of a chocolate-coconut cream pie. A lively cherry note comes into focus after the initial rush of flavor fades, making for a surprisingly satisfying counterpoint to the increasingly wood-forward nose. The combined sweet-and-savory quality never feels standard-issue, and it gives the whiskey a ton of depth, almost lip-smackingly inviting, particularly at a wholly approachable 97 proof.

There’s a reprise of wood and some black pepper, then dried mint, on the modest but satisfying finish. It’s quite a little ride, quirky and unconventional in its own way, but a special installment in a long-running series that deserves to be discovered. So, what are you waiting for?

97 proof.

A / $200 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Released as the seventh addition to the Three Ships Master’s Collection,…

The post Review: Three Ships 6 Years Old Chenin Blanc Cask appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
South Africa’s James Sedgwick Distillery is no stranger to experimental cask finishing, and given Chenin Blanc is the country’s most widely-planted grape varietal, it was only a matter of time before someone paired these casks with a whisky to represent something uniquely South African.

Released as the seventh addition to the Three Ships Master’s Collection, this whisky is produced from column-distilled malt and aged in American oak casks of varying ages before resting in Chenin Blanc wine casks for two years.

Three Ships 6 Years Old Chenin Blanc Cask Review

The nose is bright, inviting, and strikes a beautiful balance between spirit and cask. Initially it
offers a typical bourbon cask signature, while the wine cask’s fingerprint takes a little longer
to settle. The balance of oak, malt sweetness, and vanilla, blended with the excitement of
lemon zest, peach, and grapefruit, makes for an enjoyable aromatic experience. There’s also
a perfumed note present on the nose which blends well between the fruit and oak aromas,
however, some may find it unpleasant.

On the palate, the Chenin Blanc cask finish is more evident. It hits with sweet honey and
vanilla upfront, followed by vibrant pineapple, pear, apple, and a bright citrus tang to cut
through the body and carries through to the finish. Ginger builds gradually, adding structure
rather than heat. The finish leaves behind orchard fruit, soft spice, drying oak, and a slight
minerality.

What is most impressive about this whisky is its balance. It’s easy for a wine cask to steal
some spotlight from the spirit. However, here the Chenin Blanc casks brighten the
whisky’s profile, enhancing freshness while maintaining the character of the spirit. This
finish feels purposeful rather than experimental, and this one is easily one of my favorite
wine cask finishes.

This expression reinforces Three Ships’ reputation as a leading brand of South African
whisky. This edition is distinctive without chasing novelty and offers incredible value for
money. It’s available for around $45 and should appeal to whisky enthusiasts looking for
something beyond sherry and Port finishes, or perhaps an everyday summer dram.

86 proof.

B+ / $45
